title: State v. Morris
description: Whether Isaiah Morris's right to counsel, under both the Ohio and federal Constitutions, was violated during his police interrogation, leading to the suppression of his confession.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Morris's right to counsel under the Ohio Constitution does not extend to preindictment investigatory interviews, and that Morris did not unambiguously invoke his Sixth Amendment right to counsel during the interrogation after initially waiving it.
defendant_argument: Morris argued that his right to counsel under the Ohio Constitution is broader than the Sixth Amendment and was violated by the interrogation without his lawyer, and that he unambiguously invoked his Sixth Amendment right to counsel during the interrogation.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the First District's judgment and remanded the case to the trial court with instructions to vacate its order granting Morris's motion to suppress.

title: In re L.E.S.
description: Whether R.C. 3111.95(A), which allows a consenting spouse of a woman who conceives through artificial insemination to be recognized as the natural parent, applies to unmarried same-sex couples who would have been married but for Ohio's ban on same-sex marriage, with the plaintiff arguing it does not and the defendant arguing it should be retroactively applied.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, P.S., argued that the non-spousal artificial insemination statute does not apply to unmarried couples and that the First District erred in creating a 'would have been married' standard, and that C.E.'s argument was not properly raised in the trial court.
defendant_argument: The defendant, C.E., argued that under Obergefell and Pavan, the non-spousal artificial insemination statute should be interpreted gender-neutrally and applied retroactively to unmarried same-sex partners if they 'would have been married' but for Ohio's ban on same-sex marriage.
decision_outcome: The Ohio Supreme Court reversed the First District Court of Appeals' judgment, holding that Ohio's parentage statutes do not authorize a trial court to determine if C.E. and P.S. 'would have been married' and remanded the case for consideration of other issues.

title: State ex rel. Boggs v. City of Cleveland
description: Whether a property owner has standing to pursue a mandamus action to compel a foreign municipality to institute appropriation proceedings for compensation when the alleged taking occurred outside the municipality's corporate limits, with the plaintiff arguing they do have standing based on constitutional rights and the defendant arguing they do not due to lack of municipal authority outside its boundaries.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that she has standing because the Ohio Constitution guarantees compensation for private property taken for public use, regardless of whether the property is located within the taking municipality's jurisdiction, and that R.C. 719.01 allows a municipality to acquire property outside its jurisdiction for airport purposes.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the plaintiff lacked standing because a municipality has no authority to appropriate property outside its boundaries without specific statutory authorization, and that R.C. 719.01(O) does not apply to the plaintiff's property.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the judgment of the court of appeals, holding that Boggs has standing to pursue her mandamus claim, and remanded the case for consideration of the statute-of-limitations argument and then the merits of the taking claim.

title: Gatehouse Media Ohio Holdings v. City of Columbus Police Department
description: Whether police officers, when targeted by a criminal offender during a shootout while on duty, are considered 'victims' under Marsy's Law, thereby exempting their identifying information from public disclosure in bodycam and dashcam footage.
plaintiff_argument: The Columbus Dispatch argued that police officers, because they were on duty, cannot be considered 'victims' under Marsy's Law, and therefore their identifying information in bodycam and dashcam footage should not be redacted from public records.
defendant_argument: The Columbus Police Department (CPD) contended that the police officers involved in the shootout were victims of a crime under Marsy's Law, and thus their identifying information in the footage is exempt from public disclosure under the Public Records Act.
decision_outcome: The court denied the Dispatch's request for a writ of mandamus, ruling that police officers can be victims under Marsy's Law and their identifying information can be redacted from public records.

title: Lyon v. Riverside Methodist Hospital
description: Whether R.C. 2323.43, the medical claim damage cap statute, is unconstitutional as applied to the plaintiff, Susana Lyon, who suffered catastrophic injuries from medical negligence, thereby limiting her noneconomic damages.
plaintiff_argument: Susana Lyon argued that the noneconomic damages cap in R.C. 2323.43 is unconstitutional, both facially and as applied to her case, as it violates her rights to due process, equal protection, and trial by jury, and is unconstitutionally vague.
defendant_argument: The defendants-appellants argued that the trial court erred in declaring R.C. 2323.43 unconstitutional and sought to apply the $500,000 noneconomic damages cap to the jury's verdict, contending that damage caps are necessary to mitigate public interest concerns and protect the viability of the medical profession.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's judgment, finding R.C. 2323.43 unconstitutional as applied to Susana Lyon's case because the significant reduction in her noneconomic damages was unreasonable and arbitrary, violating her constitutional rights to due process and equal protection.

title: State ex rel. Martens v. Findlay Municipal Court
description: Whether George Martens has standing to challenge the jurisdiction of municipal courts over tax cases, specifically whether the public-right doctrine (from Sheward) or taxpayer standing applies to bypass the traditional personal injury requirement.
plaintiff_argument: Martens argued he had standing based on the public-right doctrine established in Sheward or, alternatively, as a taxpayer because the courts were illegally expending money.
defendant_argument: The defendant courts argued Martens lacked standing because he had not suffered a personal injury and did not meet the requirements for taxpayer standing.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the dismissal of Martens's complaint, ruling that he lacked standing, expressly overruling the Sheward public-right doctrine, and finding no taxpayer standing.

title: In Re Application for Correction of Birth Record of Hailey Emmeline Adelaide
description: Whether R.C. 3705.15 permits probate courts to correct the sex marker on a transgender person's birth certificate.
plaintiff_argument: The statute should be broadly interpreted to allow correction of the sex marker on her birth certificate, and denying it is discriminatory.
defendant_argument: The statute only allows corrections for errors made at the time of birth, not for changes in fact or circumstance that occur after birth, thus not authorizing the requested change.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court could not reach a majority consensus, leaving the Second District Court of Appeals' judgment, which affirmed the denial of Adelaide's application, undisturbed.

title: Cincinnati Enquirer v. Bloom
description: Whether the Ohio Constitution's open courts provision prohibits the mandatory sealing of juvenile delinquency records without an individualized balancing of interests, or if public access protections do not apply to such proceedings.
plaintiff_argument: The Cincinnati Enquirer argued that R.C. 2151.356 is unconstitutional because it mandates sealing records without balancing public and juvenile interests, and that the Ohio Constitution's open courts provision requires such balancing for juvenile delinquency proceedings.
defendant_argument: Judge Bloom argued that public access protections of the open courts provision do not apply to juvenile delinquency proceedings, and that the Ohio Constitution provides no greater right of public access than the First Amendment.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the open courts provision of the Ohio Constitution requires an individualized determination balancing interests before closing juvenile delinquency proceedings, and thus R.C. 2151.356 cannot be constitutionally applied without it. Writs of mandamus and prohibition were granted, ordering Judge Bloom to provide the transcript and stop enforcing the sealing order.

title: Hild, Administration of the Estate of Boldman v. Samaritan Health Partners
description: Whether the "same-juror rule" or the "any-juror rule" applies in negligence cases, specifically regarding whether only jurors who find negligence may vote on the issue of proximate cause.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the "same-juror rule" was erroneous and deprived her of the right to a full jury deliberation, advocating for the "any-juror rule" where all jurors could vote on proximate cause regardless of their negligence finding.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the "same-juror rule" logically applies to issues of negligence and proximate causation in medical negligence cases, and that courts must instruct juries to follow this rule.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Second District Court of Appeals' judgment, reinstated the trial court's denial of the plaintiff's motion for a new trial, and upheld the jury verdict in favor of the defendants.

title: State ex rel. Citizens Not Politicians v. Ohio Ballot Board
description: Whether the ballot language and ballot title for a proposed constitutional amendment, intended to create an appointed redistricting commission, are misleading, deceptive, or fraudulent to voters.
plaintiff_argument: The ballot language and title are misleading, inaccurate, and impermissibly argumentative, failing to properly identify the substance of the proposal and potentially defrauding voters.
defendant_argument: The ballot language and title are factually accurate, do not amount to impermissible persuasive argument, and properly identify the substance of the proposed amendment.
decision_outcome: The court granted a limited writ of mandamus, ordering the Ohio Ballot Board and Secretary of State to revise specific misleading parts of the ballot language concerning judicial review scope and public participation rights, but denied other requested revisions and upheld the ballot title.

title: State v. Carter
description: Whether a criminal defendant's Sixth Amendment right to face-to-face confrontation is violated when a witness testifies remotely via video conference without sufficient case-specific findings of necessity, and if so, whether such an error is harmless.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that remote testimony was justified due to increased COVID-19 spread and uncertain weather conditions, and that surging COVID-19 cases amounted to a public policy concern justifying the remote testimony.
defendant_argument: Eli Carter argued that the remote testimony of a witness via video conference, especially with speech-to-text captioning, violated his constitutional right to face-to-face confrontation.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of the Third District Court of Appeals, concluding that while the trial court erred in allowing remote testimony, this error was harmless given the overwhelming evidence of guilt.

title: Smith v. Ohio State University
description: Whether discretionary immunity is a jurisdictional bar or an affirmative defense to suits brought against the state or its instrumentalities.
plaintiff_argument: Smith argued that discretionary immunity is an affirmative defense, meaning the Court of Claims has jurisdiction to hear the case and determine if immunity applies as a defense.
defendant_argument: Ohio State University argued that discretionary immunity is a jurisdictional bar, meaning the Court of Claims lacks subject-matter jurisdiction if immunity applies.
decision_outcome: The court held that discretionary immunity is a jurisdictional bar, not an affirmative defense, and reversed the Tenth District's judgment, remanding the case to determine if discretionary immunity applies to Ohio State's actions.

title: Schaad v. Alder
description: Whether the General Assembly violated the Due Process Clause by directing that an Ohio citizen pay taxes to the municipality where the employee's principal place of work was located rather than to the subdivision of the state where the employee actually worked.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Josh Schaad, argued that Section 29 of H.B. 197 violates the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment by authorizing a municipality to tax a nonresident for work performed outside that municipality.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Karen Alder (Cincinnati's finance director), denied Schaad's tax refund request, implying the temporary law was constitutional and the tax was valid, a stance affirmed by lower courts.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of the First District Court of Appeals, ruling that Section 29 of H.B. 197 is constitutional and a valid exercise of the General Assembly's authority.

title: Everhart v. Coshocton County Memorial Hospital
description: Whether the medical-claim statute of repose, set forth under R.C. 2305.113(C), applies to statutory wrongful death claims.
plaintiff_argument: The medical-claim statute of repose does not apply to wrongful-death claims, as they are distinct from medical-malpractice claims and governed by a separate statutory chapter.
defendant_argument: The medical-claim statute of repose applies to wrongful-death claims because the broad definition of "medical claim" in the statute includes such claims.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the medical-claim statute of repose applies to wrongful-death claims based on medical care, reversing the Tenth District Court of Appeals' decision.

title: In re: Application of Alamo Solar I
description: Whether the Ohio Power Siting Board lawfully and reasonably granted certificates for the construction of two large solar farms, given concerns raised by citizens regarding environmental impact, noise, visual impact, wildlife, flooding, and setbacks.
plaintiff_argument: The citizens argued that the board erred by issuing certificates without sufficient information about noise levels, visual impact, wildlife, plants, flooding, stormwater runoff, and pollution, and by accepting unreasonably narrow setbacks, thus failing to ensure minimum adverse environmental impact.
defendant_argument: The Power Siting Board and the solar farms argued that the board's orders were lawful and reasonable, that the applications complied with regulations, and that the board's determinations regarding environmental impact were supported by evidence.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Power Siting Board's orders granting the certificates for the construction of the solar farms.

title: State v. Daniel
description: Whether R.C. 2909.15(D)(2)(b), which ties a judge's ability to reduce an arson offender's registration period to a recommendation from executive-branch officials, unconstitutionally violates the doctrine of separation of powers.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Daniel, argued that the reduced-registration provision unconstitutionally infringes on the judicial power to impose a criminal sentence and limits judicial review, thereby violating the separation-of-powers doctrine.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the State of Ohio, argued that the arson registration statute is not punitive and its registration requirements do not constitute an aspect of a criminal sentence, thus posing no separation-of-powers problem.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of the Sixth District Court of Appeals, holding that Ohio's arson-offender-registration scheme does not violate the separation-of-powers doctrine.

title: Bennett et al. v. Ohio Redistricting Commission et al.
description: Whether the Ohio Supreme Court should retain jurisdiction to review the constitutionality of the September 2023 General Assembly-districting plan, given its bipartisan support, or dismiss the cases and relinquish jurisdiction.
plaintiff_argument: Petitioners argued that the September 2023 plan, despite bipartisan approval, is a partisan gerrymander violating Article XI, Section 6(B) of the Ohio Constitution, and the court should retain jurisdiction to review it.
defendant_argument: Respondents argued that the bipartisan adoption of the September 2023 plan constitutes a changed circumstance, rendering the original complaints moot, and therefore the court should dismiss the cases and relinquish its continuing jurisdiction.
decision_outcome: The court granted the respondents' motions to dismiss the cases, denied the motions to vacate as moot, and denied the petitioners' motions for leave to file objections to the September 2023 plan.

title: League of Women Voters Ohio et al. v. Ohio Redistricting Commission et al.
description: Whether the Ohio Supreme Court should retain jurisdiction to review the constitutionality of the September 2023 General Assembly-districting plan, given its bipartisan support, or dismiss the cases and relinquish jurisdiction.
plaintiff_argument: Petitioners argued that the September 2023 plan, despite bipartisan approval, is a partisan gerrymander violating Article XI, Section 6(B) of the Ohio Constitution, and the court should retain jurisdiction to review it.
defendant_argument: Respondents argued that the bipartisan adoption of the September 2023 plan constitutes a changed circumstance, rendering the original complaints moot, and therefore the court should dismiss the cases and relinquish its continuing jurisdiction.
decision_outcome: The court granted the respondents' motions to dismiss the cases, denied the motions to vacate as moot, and denied the petitioners' motions for leave to file objections to the September 2023 plan.

title: State ex rel. Ohioans United for Reproductive Rights v. Ohio Ballot Board
description: Whether the ballot language adopted by the Ohio Ballot Board for a proposed constitutional amendment (Issue 1) is misleading, contains material omissions, or is improperly argumentative.
plaintiff_argument: The relators argued that the ballot language was misleading, contained material omissions, and was improperly argumentative, specifically citing the use of "citizens of the State" instead of "the State," "reproductive medical treatment" instead of "reproductive decisions," the omission of other reproductive decisions, and the use of terms like "unborn child" and absolute modifiers.
defendant_argument: The respondents argued that the ballot language properly identified the substance of the proposal, was not misleading, and was not improperly argumentative, asserting that "citizens of the State" is synonymous with "the State" in governmental power, and that other terms were factually accurate or imprecise but not misleading.
decision_outcome: The court granted a limited writ of mandamus, agreeing with the relators that the term "citizens of the State" in the ballot language was misleading and ordering the ballot board to change it to "the State." All other claims by the relators were denied.

title: Ohio Organizing Collaborative v. Ohio Redistricting Commission
description: Whether the Ohio Supreme Court should retain jurisdiction to review the constitutionality of the September 2023 General Assembly-districting plan, given its bipartisan support, or dismiss the cases and relinquish jurisdiction.
plaintiff_argument: Petitioners argued that the September 2023 plan, despite bipartisan approval, is a partisan gerrymander violating Article XI, Section 6(B) of the Ohio Constitution, and the court should retain jurisdiction to review it.
defendant_argument: Respondents argued that the bipartisan adoption of the September 2023 plan constitutes a changed circumstance, rendering the original complaints moot, and therefore the court should dismiss the cases and relinquish its continuing jurisdiction.
decision_outcome: The court granted the respondents' motions to dismiss the cases, denied the motions to vacate as moot, and denied the petitioners' motions for leave to file objections to the September 2023 plan.

title: State v. Hacker
description: Whether the Reagan Tokes Law, which establishes indefinite sentencing, is unconstitutional because it violates the separation-of-powers doctrine, the offender's right to a jury trial, and procedural due process.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Ohio (appellee) argued that the Reagan Tokes Law is constitutional and does not violate the separation-of-powers doctrine, the right to a jury trial, or procedural due process.
defendant_argument: Hacker and Simmons (appellants) argued that the Reagan Tokes Law is unconstitutional because it violates the separation-of-powers doctrine, the offender's right to a jury trial, and procedural due process.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Ohio affirmed the judgments of the Third and Eighth District Courts of Appeals, ruling that the Reagan Tokes Law is constitutional.

title: State ex rel. One Person One Vote v. LaRose
description: Whether the Ohio General Assembly may call for a special election on a legislatively-initiated constitutional amendment on any date, or if it is bound by existing statutes establishing when special elections may generally be held.
plaintiff_argument: The General Assembly is bound by statutes (H.B. 458) that specify when special elections can be held, and the August 8 special election is not authorized by these laws, thus violating the Ohio Constitution and state law.
defendant_argument: Article XVI, Section 1 of the Ohio Constitution authorizes the General Assembly to "prescribe" a special election on a proposed constitutional amendment by joint resolution, allowing it to set the date without being bound by general election statutes.
decision_outcome: The court denied the writ of mandamus, ruling that the August 8, 2023 special election called by the General Assembly is constitutionally valid and can proceed.

title: The State ex rel. One Person One Vote v. Ohio Ballot Board
description: Whether the ballot language and title adopted for a proposed constitutional amendment are incomplete and misleading, and whether the ballot board and Secretary of State should be compelled to adopt new, accurate language.
plaintiff_argument: The relators argued that the ballot language and title were incomplete and misleading because they failed to inform voters about current law, mischaracterized signature requirements, and used prejudicial language like "elevating standards" and "any constitutional amendment."
defendant_argument: The Ohio Ballot Board and Secretary of State Frank LaRose contended that the adopted ballot language and title properly identified the substance of the proposed amendment and were not misleading, deceptive, or fraudulent.
decision_outcome: The court granted the writ of mandamus in part, ordering the ballot board to adopt new language accurately defining "electors" for petition signatures and Secretary LaRose to remove the word "any" from the ballot title when referring to "constitutional amendment." The court denied the writ for other claims, including the need to describe current law or change the word "elevating."

title: State ex rel. DeBlase v. Ohio Ballot Board
description: Whether an initiative petition proposing a constitutional amendment titled "The Right to Reproductive Freedom with Protections for Health and Safety" contains a single constitutional amendment or multiple amendments that should be divided, with plaintiffs arguing for division and defendants arguing it is a single amendment.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the initiative petition contains more than one proposed constitutional amendment because it groups abortion with other reproductive decisions, claiming abortion is a unique act, and because it encompasses both broad constitutional rights and specific legislative details.
defendant_argument: The defendants, supported by the court's reasoning, argued that the petition contains a single constitutional amendment because all its provisions relate to the common purpose of protecting reproductive rights, and the Ohio Constitution does not limit amendments to only broad principles.
decision_outcome: The court denied the writ of mandamus, ruling that the Ohio Ballot Board did not abuse its discretion or disregard applicable law in determining that the initiative petition proposes only one constitutional amendment.

title: State ex rel. Ware v. Parikh
description: Whether an inmate's request for judges' oaths of office and specific court records should be granted under Ohio's Public Records Act, or if the oaths are governed by the Rules of Superintendence and the court records are exempt under R.C. 149.43(B)(8).
plaintiff_argument: Ware argued he was entitled to both categories of records under the Public Records Act and sought a writ of mandamus.
defendant_argument: Parikh argued the oaths were governed by the Rules of Superintendence, not the Public Records Act, and the other court records were exempt under R.C. 149.43(B)(8) because they related to a criminal investigation/prosecution case initiated before July 1, 2009.
decision_outcome: The court granted the writ of mandamus in part, ordering the clerk to produce the requested records from the Cincinnati Enquirer case and awarding Ware $1,000 in statutory damages and court costs, but denied the writ for the judges' oaths of office.

title: Brandt v. Pompa
description: Whether the compensatory-damages caps for noneconomic loss in R.C. 2315.18 are unconstitutional as applied to appellant, Amanda Brandt, with the plaintiff arguing they are unconstitutional and the defendant arguing they are constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Amanda Brandt, argued that the statutory caps on noneconomic damages are unconstitutional as applied to her case because they arbitrarily exclude severe psychological injuries from exceptions, violating the due-course-of-law guarantee.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Roy Pompa, argued that the statutory damages caps in R.C. 2315.18 are constitutional and should be applied, as the General Assembly has the right to set such caps to protect the economy and prevent inflated awards.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that R.C. 2315.18's compensatory-damages caps for noneconomic loss are unconstitutional as applied to Brandt, reversing the appellate court's judgment and reinstating the jury's original damages award.

title: McClain v. State
description: Whether a defendant is entitled to a jury trial under Article I, Section 5 of the Ohio Constitution in a claim for wrongful imprisonment, with the plaintiff arguing for the right to a jury trial and the defendant arguing against it.
plaintiff_argument: McClain argued that a wrongful-imprisonment claim has roots in the common law tort of false imprisonment, which carried a right to a jury trial, thus entitling him to a jury trial.
defendant_argument: The state argued that McClain's claim is statutory, has no common-law analogue, seeks relief unavailable at common law, and that the state cannot be sued without its express consent, which does not include a jury trial for this new cause of action.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of the First District Court of Appeals, holding that Anthony McClain has no constitutional right to a jury trial in his action to be declared a wrongfully imprisoned person under R.C. 2743.48.

title: State v. Brasher
description: Whether a trial court retains jurisdiction to impose restitution on a defendant after the defendant has completed their prison sentence and the original sentencing judgment has become final, or if victims must appeal the initial denial of restitution directly.
plaintiff_argument: Victims are constitutionally entitled to full and timely restitution under Marsy's Law and should have an effective appellate remedy, including seeking a writ of mandamus, even after the defendant's sentence is completed.
defendant_argument: The trial court loses jurisdiction to modify a sentence once it is final and the defendant has completed their prison term, and imposing restitution afterward violates Double Jeopardy. Victims should have pursued a direct appeal.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Ohio affirmed the judgment of the Twelfth District Court of Appeals, ruling that the trial court's later order of restitution was void because it lacked jurisdiction to modify the sentence after it became final and the defendant had completed his prison term.

title: State v. Morris
description: Whether a trial court that sentences a juvenile defendant to life in prison without considering their youth as a mitigating factor violates the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments to the United States Constitution and Article I, Section 9 of the Ohio Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Morris argued that the trial court failed to consider his youth as a mitigating factor in sentencing, which constitutes cruel and unusual punishment under both the Ohio and federal constitutions, as required by *State v. Patrick*.
defendant_argument: The Ohio Attorney General (amicus curiae for the state) argued that neither the United States Constitution nor the Ohio Constitution requires a trial court to consider a juvenile offender's age on the record before sentencing to a life sentence with parole, and that *Jones v. Mississippi* effectively overruled *State v. Patrick*.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the judgment of the Fifth District Court of Appeals, holding that Morris's sentence constitutes cruel and unusual punishment, and remanded the case to the trial court to vacate the sentence and resentence him after considering his youth as a mitigating factor.

title: In re D.R.
description: Whether R.C. 2152.84, which mandates continued Tier I sex offender classification for 16- and 17-year-old juvenile offenders without judicial discretion at the completion-of-disposition hearing, violates due process.
plaintiff_argument: D.R. argues that R.C. 2152.84 is unconstitutional as applied to him because it removes judicial discretion to terminate his sex offender classification at the completion-of-disposition hearing, violating his due process rights.
defendant_argument: The state argues that R.C. 2152.84 is fundamentally fair and complies with due process, as it provides an initial classification hearing with discretion and allows for a review to terminate registration after three years.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the appellate court's decision, ruling that R.C. 2152.84(A)(2)(b) is unconstitutional as applied to D.R. because it removes judicial discretion at the completion-of-disposition hearing, violating due process. The case was remanded for a new hearing.

title: State v. Haynes
description: Whether the state is required to provide a bill of particulars upon a defendant's request, or if open-file discovery can serve as a substitute.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Ohio argued that open-file discovery was sufficient and a bill of particulars was not required when discovery was provided.
defendant_argument: Haynes argued that he had a constitutional right to a bill of particulars upon request, and the state's failure to provide one hampered his defense.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the judgment of the Sixth District Court of Appeals, vacated Haynes's conviction, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: State v. Yerkey
description: Whether a crime victim is entitled to receive restitution from an offender for wages lost as a result of the victim's choice to exercise her right to attend court hearings.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Ohio argued that Marsy's Law provides a constitutional right to full and timely restitution, which includes lost wages incurred by victims attending court proceedings.
defendant_argument: John Yerkey argued that restitution in Ohio law is limited to economic losses directly and proximately caused by the offense, and lost wages for voluntarily attending court hearings do not qualify.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Ohio affirmed the judgment of the Seventh District Court of Appeals, ruling that lost wages incurred by a victim for attending court hearings are not compensable as restitution under Ohio law.

title: State ex rel. Maras v. LaRose
description: Whether Ohio Revised Code 3505.21, which governs the appointment of election observers, violates the Equal Protection Clauses of the United States and Ohio Constitutions by restricting independent candidates' ability to appoint observers and denying observers access to election machine software, or if the statute is constitutional and rationally related to a legitimate government interest.
plaintiff_argument: Maras argues that R.C. 3505.21 unconstitutionally restricts independent candidates from appointing election observers to the same extent as political parties and denies observers access to election machine software and source codes, which she deems essential for meaningful observation and election integrity.
defendant_argument: Secretary LaRose argues that R.C. 3505.21 is constitutional under rational-basis review, as it does not treat candidates differently based on party affiliation for observer appointments, and there is no statutory right for observers to inspect election machine software/hardware or demand hand-tallying.
decision_outcome: The court denied the writ of mandamus sought by Maras, upholding the constitutionality of R.C. 3505.21 and affirming that there is no statutory right for election observers to inspect election machine software or demand hand-tallying.

title: State ex rel. Sanduskians for Sandusky v. The City of Sandusky
description: Whether R.C. 731.31, which requires initiative petitions to contain the full text of a proposed measure, applies to a petition to amend a city charter, with relators arguing it does not and city respondents arguing it does.
plaintiff_argument: The relators argued that the Sandusky Charter's Section 82 governs charter amendments and does not require the full-text provision of R.C. 731.31, making their petition valid.
defendant_argument: The city respondents argued that R.C. 731.31 applies to charter-amendment petitions, and since the relators' petition lacked the full text of the proposed amendment, it was insufficient.
decision_outcome: The court granted a limited writ of mandamus, ordering the Sandusky City Commission to enact an ordinance for the submission of the proposed charter amendment to the electors at a special election, provided the petition has enough valid signatures, but denied the request for attorney fees and placement on the November 8, 2022 ballot.

title: Neiman v. LaRose
description: Whether the congressional-district plan adopted by the Ohio Redistricting Commission on March 2, 2022, unduly favors or disfavors a political party in violation of Article XIX, Section 1(C)(3)(a) of the Ohio Constitution, with petitioners arguing it is an unconstitutional partisan gerrymander and respondents arguing it is constitutional and aims for competitive districts.
plaintiff_argument: The March 2 plan unduly favors the Republican Party and disfavors the Democratic Party, violating Article XIX, Section 1(C)(3)(a) of the Ohio Constitution, as evidenced by expert analyses showing it to be a partisan outlier that packs Democratic voters and is less compact.
defendant_argument: The March 2 plan is constitutional, as the commission is not necessarily bound by the same anti-gerrymandering provisions as the General Assembly, and the plan reasonably attempts to maximize competitive seats; furthermore, petitioners failed to prove their case beyond a reasonable doubt.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the March 2 congressional-district plan is invalid because it unduly favors the Republican Party in violation of Article XIX, Section 1(C)(3)(a) of the Ohio Constitution, and ordered the General Assembly to pass a new compliant plan within 30 days.

title: State ex rel. Demora v. LaRose
description: Whether the statutory filing deadlines for primary election candidates automatically shifted when a federal court ordered a new primary election date, or if the original deadlines remained in effect.
plaintiff_argument: The original relators argued that statutory filing deadlines are tied to the actual primary election date, and since the August 2 primary was set, their declarations filed in May were timely according to R.C. 3513.05 and 3513.041.
defendant_argument: Secretary LaRose argued that the original February filing deadlines remained in effect, and the federal court order moving the primary date did not reopen or alter these deadlines, making later filings untimely and void.
decision_outcome: The court granted the writ of mandamus for the original relators, compelling the Secretary of State and county boards of elections to accept their declarations of candidacy and petitions as timely and certify them to the August 2 primary ballot if they otherwise qualify. The court denied the writ of mandamus for the intervening relators.

title: The Village of Newburgh Heights v. State
description: Whether the Ohio Constitution's Home Rule Amendment prohibits the General Assembly from enacting statutes that reduce a municipality's share of local-government funds based on traffic camera fines and require an advance deposit for civil actions to enforce traffic camera citations.
plaintiff_argument: The municipalities argued that the spending setoff and deposit requirement unconstitutionally penalize them for exercising their home-rule authority to enforce traffic laws with cameras.
defendant_argument: The State of Ohio argued that the General Assembly has the constitutional authority to enact these statutes, which do not infringe upon municipal home-rule powers.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the judgment of the Eighth District Court of Appeals, holding that the spending setoff and the deposit requirement are constitutional and do not violate municipal home-rule powers.

title: State v. McAlpin
description: Whether Joseph McAlpin's convictions and death sentence should be overturned due to alleged errors in his capital trial, including issues with his right to self-representation, standby counsel's interference, admission of evidence, prosecutorial misconduct, jury selection, and sentencing procedures.
plaintiff_argument: McAlpin argued that various errors, including the denial of his right to self-representation in all capital trial phases, interference by standby counsel, improper admission of evidence, prosecutorial misconduct, and flawed jury instructions, deprived him of a fair trial and rendered his death sentence unreliable.
defendant_argument: The State argued that McAlpin's rights were not violated, that any alleged errors did not constitute plain error or prejudice the outcome, and that the evidence overwhelmingly supported his convictions and death sentence.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Ohio affirmed Joseph McAlpin's convictions for aggravated murder and his sentence of death.

title: Siltstone Res. v. Ohio Public Works Commission
description: Whether a deed's transfer restriction, requiring prior consent for alienation of property acquired with public funds for conservation, is a valid and enforceable restraint on alienation.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Siltstone Resources, L.L.C., and other appellants argued that the transfer restriction is an invalid and unreasonable restraint on alienation, and that the Ohio Public Works Commission's remedies should be limited to liquidated damages, not injunctive relief.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Ohio Public Works Commission (OPWC), argued that the transfer restriction is valid, reasonable, and serves a public purpose, and that the Guernsey County Community Development Corporation (CDC) violated it by transferring mineral rights without OPWC's consent, entitling OPWC to equitable remedies.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the appellate court's judgment, holding that the transfer restriction in the deed was valid and enforceable, and that the state was entitled to remedies for its violation.

title: Adams v. DeWine
description: Whether the congressional-district plan unduly favors a political party or its incumbents and unduly splits governmental units in violation of Article XIX, Section 1(C)(3)(a) and (b) of the Ohio Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that the enacted congressional-district plan unduly favors the Republican Party and disfavors the Democratic Party, and unduly splits governmental units like Hamilton, Cuyahoga, and Summit Counties for partisan advantage, violating Article XIX of the Ohio Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the plan is constitutional, maximizes competitive districts, complies with Article XIX's splitting rules, and that the constitutional provisions do not provide a judicially manageable standard for determining "undue" favoritism or splitting.
decision_outcome: The court declared the congressional-district plan invalid and ordered the General Assembly to pass a new, compliant plan.

title: DuBose v. McGuffey
description: Whether the trial court's $1,500,000 bail for Justin DuBose was unconstitutionally excessive, and whether the court of appeals correctly applied de novo review and disregarded public safety concerns when reducing it.
plaintiff_argument: The $1,500,000 bail was excessive and effectively a denial of bail, as he and his family could not afford it, and it did not properly consider his financial resources, community ties, and lack of felony record.
defendant_argument: The court of appeals erred by reviewing the bail decision de novo instead of for abuse of discretion, and by discounting the victim's family's safety concerns. The bail was appropriate given the serious nature of the crime, DuBose's alleged flight risk, and public safety concerns.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Ohio affirmed the judgment of the court of appeals, which had reduced DuBose's bail from $1,500,000 to $500,000, finding the original amount unconstitutionally excessive.

title: The Cleveland Electric Illuminating Co. v. The City of Cleveland
description: Whether a municipality violates Article XVIII, Section 6 of the Ohio Constitution by selling an "artificial surplus" of electricity (electricity purchased solely for extraterritorial resale) to customers outside its boundaries, with the plaintiff arguing it is unconstitutional and the defendant arguing it is permissible under home-rule authority.
plaintiff_argument: The city's sale of electricity to Brooklyn constitutes an "artificial surplus" acquired solely for extraterritorial resale, which violates Article XVIII, Sections 4 and 6 of the Ohio Constitution, as a municipality may only sell surplus electricity it produces and not electricity purchased solely for resale.
defendant_argument: A municipality is permitted to sell surplus electricity extraterritorially up to 50% of its total service, and it may acquire excess capacity for various legitimate reasons (cost, risk mitigation, economies of scale, environmental impact, reliability, and PJM reserve margin requirements) other than solely for extraterritorial resale, without violating the Ohio Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Eighth District Court of Appeals' judgment, which reversed the trial court's grant of summary judgment in favor of the city and remanded the case for further proceedings due to existing issues of material fact.

title: State ex rel. Suwalski v. Peeler
description: Whether a common pleas court judge has the judicial power to restore federal firearms rights to a person convicted of misdemeanor domestic violence, and whether the victim has standing to challenge such an order under Marsy's Law.
plaintiff_argument: Judge Peeler lacked the judicial power to restore federal firearms rights to Roy Ewing, and his order violated Jamie Suwalski's rights as a crime victim to safety and protection under Marsy's Law, giving her the right to challenge it.
defendant_argument: Judge Peeler's order restoring Roy Ewing's firearms rights was proper, Suwalski failed to exhaust her claims, Marsy's Law is not applicable, and her action is barred by res judicata.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the court of appeals' judgment, granting a writ of prohibition that invalidated Judge Peeler's order restoring Roy Ewing's federal firearms rights, finding that the order was unauthorized by law and that victim Jamie Suwalski had no other adequate remedy.

title: State v. Jordan
description: Whether a police officer is constitutionally required to secure an arrest warrant before conducting a public felony arrest when it is practicable to do so.
plaintiff_argument: Jordan argued that a warrantless arrest is unconstitutional if there is an unreasonable delay in effecting the arrest, or if it was practicable to obtain a warrant.
defendant_argument: The State argued that a warrantless arrest based on probable cause in a public place does not violate the Fourth Amendment, and neither exigent circumstances nor impracticability of obtaining a warrant is necessary.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of the First District Court of Appeals, holding that a warrantless public arrest based on probable cause is constitutionally valid and does not require exigent circumstances or impracticability of obtaining a warrant.

title: State v. Hubbard
description: Whether the retroactive application of "Sierah's Law" to offenders who committed their offenses prior to the law's effective date violates the Retroactivity Clause of the Ohio Constitution, with the plaintiff arguing it is remedial and the defendant arguing it is punitive.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Ohio argued that Sierah's Law is remedial, not punitive, and therefore its retroactive application does not violate the Ohio Constitution's Retroactivity Clause, as it does not impair vested rights or impose new burdens.
defendant_argument: Hubbard argued that Sierah's Law imposes new, punitive burdens, duties, obligations, and liabilities that did not exist at the time he committed his offense, thereby violating the Ohio Constitution's Retroactivity Clause.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of the Twelfth District Court of Appeals, ruling that the retroactive application of Sierah's Law does not violate the Retroactivity Clause of the Ohio Constitution.
